newsitem.title: USA: Progress reported in talks to end GM plant strike.
newsitem.headline: Progress reported in talks to end GM plant strike.

text.p: Progress was reported in a three-day old General Motors Corp. parts plant strike on Friday that has already forced the shutdown of six assembly plants, affecting nearly 17,000 workers in the United States and Canada.
"We're hearing that we're close but that we're not quite there yet," said Jim Marcum, financial secretary for United Auto Worker Local 909 in Warren, Mich.
"It could go five minutes. It could go another five days," he said.
About 2,800 members of Local 909 walked off the job at midnight on Tuesday when talks on a new three-year contract failed to produce an agreement by the strike deadline.
The plant makes automatic transmissions for many of GM's front-wheel drive cars and light trucks, as well as wheels and suspension control arms.

Analysts on Friday were generally predicting a settlement sooner rather than later. But even a one-week shutdown will hold back growth in the Detroit and Michigan economy, said David Littmann, chief economist of Comerica Bank, a unit of Comerica Inc.

If the strike lasts two weeks, Littmann predicted, it will start to have a national impact, driving up first-time unemployment claims by 20,000, and shaving half a percentage point from the industrial production index.
"Beyond that, it's a wholesale disaster for GM earnings," he said.
Strikes cost the world's largest automaker lost profits of $490 million in the second quarter, and $1.2 billion in all of 1996.

Union officials said on Thursday that some progress has been made on staffing issues. The union reportedly wants the automaker to add between 250 and 400 jobs to make up for retirements and ease overtime burdens.

However, the two sides are still at odds over GM's desire to move production of wheels out of Warren. Sources close to the talks said GM has offered to make up for the wheel work by moving torque converters, used in auto transmissions, into Warren. But that move means the torque production would be lost by GM's UAW-staffed Buick City complex in Flint, Mich.

The strike has forced the temporary shutdown of plants in Lansing, Orion Township, and Flint, Mich. Those plants make the Buick LaSabre, Buick Riviera, Oldsmobile Aurora, Oldsmobile Achieva, Oldsmobile Eighty Eight, Pontiac Grand Am, Pontiac Bonneville, and Chevrolet Cavalier.

In addition, an assembly complex in Oshawa, Ontario, with two assembly lines shut down on Friday morning. The facility produces the Chevrolet Lumina and Chevrolet Monte Carlo, and the Buick Park Avenue, Regal and Century sedans.

GM spokesman Tom Klipstine said there are not likely to be any more shutdowns until next week. Analysts said production at the Doraville, Ga., plant that supplies GM's new minivans to both the United States and Europe could be halted by Tuesday because of a shortage of transmissions.

Starting on Wednesday, several car plants could go down, according to Mike Robinet, managing director of CSM Forecasting, an industry consultant in Farmington Hills, Mich. Those are: Fairfax, Kan., which makes the Pontiac Grand Prix and 1998 Oldsmobile Intrigue; Oklahoma City, and Wilmington, Del., which make the Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass; and Lordstown, Ohio, where the Cavalier and Pontiac Sunfire are produced.

Production at GM's pickup truck operations and additional car plants could be affected later next week. Dealers said on Friday that any disruption of truck production could have a quick ripple effect on retail sales.
"On the car side, it will take a little longer. Something that lasts a week or two probably won't affect retail sales," said Gerald Seiner, president of a group of GM dealerships in Salt Lake City.

GM has been on a company-wide campaign to shrink its hourly work force by 12,000 to 15,000 annually through attrition to reduce costs and become more competitive. The automaker had about 215,000 UAW workers last year.
Union leaders, trying to protect jobs and put a halt to oursourcing, have resisted those efforts. The clash has lead to six strikes against GM this year, including the Warren work stoppage.
GM's stock closed down $1.44 at $56.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
